name: Carman

attributes.attribute: one of the earliest rulers of Ireland

sources: Gwynn, Edward. The Metrical Dindshenchas. Vol. III. Royal Irish Academy, Todd Lecture Series. Dublin: Hodges, Figgis, and Co., Ltd., 1906–1924, 3-27.
MacCulloch, J. A. The Religion of the Ancient Celts. London: Constable, 1911, 167.
Raftery, Brian. Pagan Celtic Ireland: The Enigma of the Irish Iron Age. London: Thames and Hudson, 1994, 82.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Carman was an Irish goddess or heroine. Irish legend placed her among the earliest rulers of Ireland. She was a sorceress whose power was destructive. Her three sons matched her destructive nature. They were Dub, the darkness; Dothur, the wickedness; and Dian, the violence. Together the sons blighted Ireland’s corn. The people of the goddess Danu formed the Tuatha Dé Danann. They gathered enough magic to drive the sons from the land. Carman herself resisted longer. A bard could not stop her. A satirist failed as well. The sorceress Bé Chuille cast a spell strong enough to undo Carman’s energy. Carman died of grief when she heard her sons had been killed. A festival honored her despite the enmity. It was called the Óenach Carman. The site stood on the Curragh in Co. Kildare or on the plains of the River Barrow. The varied site suggests the people saw her as a force to propitiate. Similar festivals honored the goddesses Tailtiu and Tlachtga. These festivals tied the goddesses to the harvest season.

okr.objective: Carman is a destructive Irish goddess whose doomed sons blight the land.
